page: Microsoft Azure M192lds_v4 is a high-capacity memory-optimized virtual machine instance based on the Intel x86_64 processor architecture running on Microsoft Hyper-V. The system provides 192 dedicated virtual CPU cores paired with 3072 GB of system memory, yielding an allocation of 16 GB of RAM per vCPU. Hardware graphics acceleration is not included in this configuration.

For fast ephemeral storage requirements, the instance includes 7086 GB of local NVMe SSD capacity, providing rapid read and write access for local caching, index files, and temporary processing data. The instance does not bundle complimentary public IPv4 addresses, requiring routing through standard virtual network infrastructure.

The substantial memory footprint and high core count position the instance for massive memory-bound workloads. Typical operational profiles include large-scale in-memory databases such as SAP HANA, high-throughput transactional database management systems, and intensive analytical processing frameworks that require low compute contention and multi-terabyte active working memory.
description: Microsoft Azure M192lds_v4 is an enterprise memory-optimized virtual machine built on the Microsoft Hyper-V platform. It is powered by dedicated Intel x86_64 processors delivering 192 vCPUs coupled with 3072 GB of system memory, resulting in a high density of 16 GB of RAM per virtual processor. The instance incorporates 7086 GB of local NVMe SSD storage for low-latency scratch volumes and high-throughput temporary caching. It does not include dedicated graphics processing units or complimentary public IPv4 addresses. The hardware architecture emphasizes massive memory capacity alongside high dedicated CPU allocation, avoiding shared-core contention. Consequently, the M192lds_v4 is structured for resource-heavy workloads, including large-scale in-memory databases such as SAP HANA, massive relational databases, enterprise transactional systems, and demanding memory-bound analytics pipelines requiring extensive working memory.
